title: My first weeks in MDS
text:
Orientation day on campus.



My UBC Master of Data Science Orientation Experience
From August 26 to August 28, I had the opportunity to attend the UBC Master of Data Science (MDS) Orientation. It was an exciting few days filled with learning, new experiences, and meeting people who will be part of my journey at UBC.
During orientation, I got a better understanding of what the program will look like, including the course structure, timelines, expectations, and what to prepare for in the coming months. One of the highlights was learning more about the capstone projects, which gave me a glimpse into how we will apply the knowledge and skills we develop throughout the program to real-world problems.
Beyond the academic sessions, orientation was a great opportunity to make connections and build a community. I got to meet my fellow MDS students, make new friends, and connect with MDS alumni who shared their experiences and insights about the program.
And, of course, one of the most memorable moments was winning the Campus Goose Chase! It was a fun way to explore campus, work together, and create some great memories right from the beginning of my UBC journey.
Overall, the three days gave me a clearer picture of what lies ahead and made me even more excited to begin this new chapter as a UBC MDS student. I’m looking forward to learning, growing, and making many more memories along the way!

text:
The Body Condition Index

Create BCI column

penguins <- penguins %>%
  mutate(
    bci = body_mass_g / flipper_length_mm
  )
penguins %>%
  select(
    species,
    sex,
    body_mass_g,
    flipper_length_mm,
    bci
  ) %>%
  head()

# A tibble: 6 × 5
  species sex    body_mass_g flipper_length_mm   bci
  <fct>   <fct>        <int>             <int> <dbl>
1 Adelie  male          3750               181  20.7
2 Adelie  female        3800               186  20.4
3 Adelie  female        3250               195  16.7
4 Adelie  <NA>            NA                NA  NA  
5 Adelie  female        3450               193  17.9
6 Adelie  male          3650               190  19.2




Calculate BCI by species and sex with ranks

bci_profile <- penguins %>%
  group_by(species, sex) %>%
  summarise(
    bci = mean(bci, na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

bci_ranked <- bci_profile %>%
  arrange(desc(bci)) %>%
  mutate(rank = row_number())

print(bci_ranked)

# A tibble: 8 × 4
  species   sex      bci  rank
  <fct>     <fct>  <dbl> <int>
1 Gentoo    male    24.8     1
2 Gentoo    female  22.0     2
3 Gentoo    <NA>    21.3     3
4 Adelie    male    21.0     4
5 Chinstrap male    19.7     5
6 Adelie    <NA>    19.1     6
7 Chinstrap female  18.4     7
8 Adelie    female  17.9     8




Plot the Body Condition Index

ggplot(
  bci_profile,
  aes(
    x = species,
    y = bci,
    fill = sex
  )
) +
  geom_col(position = "dodge") +
  labs(
    title = "Average Body Condition Index by Species and Sex",
    x = "Species",
    y = "Average BCI",
    fill = "Sex"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()




Average Body Condition Index by Species and Sex





I calculated the overall correlation between penguin bill length and bill depth and then calculated the correlation separately for each species to examine Simpson’s paradox. The results show that the overall relationship differs from the relationships observed within individual species, demonstrating how grouping by species can change the apparent correlation.
I also calculated the Body Condition Index (BCI) as body mass divided by flipper length, then compared the average BCI across species and sex. The BCI results show differences between demographic groups, which are visible in the bar plot.

title: Milestone 3 - Python Computational Post
text:
Uncovering Simpson’s Paradox
This computation calculates the correlation between bill length and bill depth. When evaluated altogether, the variables appear negatively correlated. However, when split by species, they are highly positively correlated—a classic statistical phenomenon known as Simpson’s Paradox.

print(f"Overall Correlation: {penguins['bill_length_mm'].corr(penguins['bill_depth_mm']):.2f}")
for species, group in penguins.groupby('species'):
    spec_corr = group['bill_length_mm'].corr(group['bill_depth_mm'])
    print(f"{species} Correlation: {spec_corr:.2f}")


Overall Correlation: -0.23
Adelie Correlation: 0.39
Chinstrap Correlation: 0.65
Gentoo Correlation: 0.65



# Graph the paradox
sns.lmplot(data=penguins, x="bill_length_mm", y="bill_depth_mm", hue="species", palette="Set2")
plt.title("Simpson's Paradox: Penguin Bill Dimensions")
plt.xlabel("Bill Length (mm)")
plt.ylabel("Bill Depth (mm)")
plt.show()

title: Milestone 3 - Python Computational Post
text:
The “Body Condition Index
This block constructs a custom engineering metric: a Body Condition Index (BCI). BCI calculates how many grams of body mass a penguin carries per millimeter of flipper length, highlighting which species and sex are the most robustly built relative to their frame.

penguins['bci'] = penguins['body_mass_g'] / penguins['flipper_length_mm']

# Rank profiles by demographic subgroup
bci_profile = penguins.groupby(['species', 'sex'])['bci'].mean().reset_index()
print(bci_profile.sort_values(by='bci', ascending=False))

     species     sex        bci
5     Gentoo    male  24.762056
4     Gentoo  female  21.996526
1     Adelie    male  21.017003
3  Chinstrap    male  19.685535
2  Chinstrap  female  18.401982
0     Adelie  female  17.943739



# Graph the distribution profile
plt.figure(figsize=(8, 5))
sns.boxplot(data=penguins, x="species", y="bci", hue="sex", palette="Pastel1")
plt.title("Penguin Body Condition Profile (Mass / Flipper Ratio)")
plt.xlabel("Species")
plt.ylabel("BCI (g / mm)")
plt.show()









What we did: We loaded the dataset using the standalone package and analyzed how penguin body parts scale together.
Finding 1 (Simpson’s Paradox): If you mix all penguins together, bills look like they get flatter as they get longer. But when looked at species by species, bills actually get longer and deeper together.
Finding 2 (Body Condition): We calculated weight relative to wing size. We found that Gentoo penguins are the most robustly built species, and males are consistently bulkier than females across all species.

title: Penguin Measurements Across R and Python
text:
This analysis uses the Palmer Penguins dataset from Palmer Station Antarctica LTER.
We investigate two questions:

Does the relationship between bill length and bill depth change when penguins are grouped by species?
How does average body mass relative to flipper length differ across species and sex?

R loads the dataset and calculates the overall correlation. Python accesses the R data object, calculates species-level correlations, and creates a mass-to-flipper-length ratio. The resulting data objects return to R for ranking and visualization.

title: Penguin Measurements Across R and Python
text:
This analysis uses the Palmer Penguins dataset from Palmer Station Antarctica LTER.
We investigate two questions:

Does the relationship between bill length and bill depth change when penguins are grouped by species?
How does average body mass relative to flipper length differ across species and sex?

R loads the dataset and calculates the overall correlation. Python accesses the R data object, calculates species-level correlations, and creates a mass-to-flipper-length ratio. The resulting data objects return to R for ranking and visualization.

title: Penguin Measurements Across R and Python
text:
Setup
The document uses the knitr engine. Python chunks run through reticulate, allowing objects to be shared between languages.

library(reticulate)
library(palmerpenguins)
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)

# Use a plain data frame for straightforward conversion to pandas.
penguins_data <- as.data.frame(palmerpenguins::penguins)

title: Penguin Measurements Across R and Python
text:
Calculation 1: Overall correlation in R
We use observations with both bill measurements available.

overall_corr <- cor(
  penguins_data$bill_length_mm,
  penguins_data$bill_depth_mm,
  use = "complete.obs"
)

overall_results <- data.frame(
  complete_pairs = sum(
    complete.cases(
      penguins_data[, c("bill_length_mm", "bill_depth_mm")]
    )
  ),
  correlation = round(overall_corr, 3)
)

knitr::kable(overall_results)




complete_pairs
correlation




342
-0.235

title: Penguin Measurements Across R and Python
text:
Calculation 2: Species-level correlations in Python
The expression r.penguins_data accesses the data frame created in R. reticulate converts it to a pandas DataFrame.
We also access the R scalar overall_corr to compare the pooled correlation with the species-level results.

import pandas as pd

# Transfer the R data frame into Python.
penguins_py = r.penguins_data.copy()

correlation_rows = []

for species, group in penguins_py.groupby("species", observed=True):
    complete = group.dropna(
        subset=["bill_length_mm", "bill_depth_mm"]
    )

    correlation_rows.append({
        "species": str(species),
        "complete_pairs": len(complete),
        "correlation": complete["bill_length_mm"].corr(
            complete["bill_depth_mm"]
        )
    })

species_correlations = pd.DataFrame(correlation_rows)

print(f"Overall correlation from R: {float(r.overall_corr):.3f}")

Overall correlation from R: -0.235

print(species_correlations.round(3).to_string(index=False))

  species  complete_pairs  correlation
   Adelie             151        0.391
Chinstrap              68        0.654
   Gentoo             123        0.643


The pooled correlation is negative, but each species has a positive correlation. This reversal illustrates Simpson’s paradox: combining groups can produce a relationship that differs from the relationships within those groups.
Species differ in their typical bill dimensions, so the pooled association mixes within-species and between-species variation.

Visualizing the reversal in R
Colored lines show separate linear fits for each species. The dashed black line shows the pooled fit across all species.

bill_data <- penguins_data %>%
  filter(
    !is.na(bill_length_mm),
    !is.na(bill_depth_mm)
  )

ggplot(
  bill_data,
  aes(
    x = bill_length_mm,
    y = bill_depth_mm,
    colour = species
  )
) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.65) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE) +
  geom_smooth(
    aes(group = 1),
    method = "lm",
    se = FALSE,
    colour = "black",
    linetype = "dashed"
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Simpson's Paradox in Penguin Bill Measurements",
    subtitle = "Colored lines: species fits; dashed black line: pooled fit",
    x = "Bill length (mm)",
    y = "Bill depth (mm)",
    colour = "Species"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()







Figure 1: Bill measurements show a negative pooled association but positive associations within species.

title: Penguin Measurements Across R and Python
text:
Calculation 3: Mass-to-flipper-length ratio in Python
For consistency with the original analysis, we call this ratio BCI:
\[
\mathrm{BCI} =
\frac{\text{body mass (g)}}{\text{flipper length (mm)}}.
\]
This ratio has units of grams per millimeter. It is a descriptive measure, not a validated health indicator.
We calculate the ratio for individual penguins, then average it within species–sex groups. Records with missing sex or missing BCI are excluded from these group summaries.

penguins_bci = penguins_py.copy()

penguins_bci["bci"] = (
    penguins_bci["body_mass_g"]
    / penguins_bci["flipper_length_mm"]
)

bci_complete = penguins_bci.dropna(
    subset=["species", "sex", "bci"]
)

bci_profile = (
    bci_complete
    .groupby(["species", "sex"], observed=True)
    .agg(
        mean_bci=("bci", "mean"),
        sd_bci=("bci", "std"),
        n=("bci", "count")
    )
    .reset_index()
)

print(bci_profile.round(3).to_string(index=False))

  species    sex  mean_bci  sd_bci  n
   Adelie female    17.944   1.397 73
   Adelie   male    21.017   1.682 73
Chinstrap female    18.402   1.457 34
Chinstrap   male    19.686   1.489 34
   Gentoo female    21.997   1.187 58
   Gentoo   male    24.762   1.354 61

title: Penguin Measurements Across R and Python
section: Calculation 4: Bring Python results back into R and rank groups
text:
Calculation 4: Bring Python results back into R and rank groups
The py$ interface accesses objects created in Python. Here we retrieve both the enriched individual-level dataset and the group summary.
Groups with equal average BCI receive the same rank.

# Transfer Python data frames back into R.
penguins_enriched <- py$penguins_bci
bci_summary_r <- py$bci_profile

bci_ranked <- bci_summary_r %>%
  mutate(rank = min_rank(desc(mean_bci))) %>%
  arrange(rank, species, sex) %>%
  select(rank, species, sex, n, mean_bci, sd_bci)

knitr::kable(
  bci_ranked,
  digits = 3,
  caption = "Species–sex groups ranked by average BCI"
)

title: Penguin Measurements Across R and Python
text:
Discussion
The bill measurements demonstrate Simpson’s paradox: the overall negative correlation reverses direction when the data are analyzed within species. The pooled relationship therefore does not describe the relationship within any individual species.
Average BCI also differs across species–sex groups. However, a larger ratio should not automatically be interpreted as better condition. Species and sexes differ naturally in body size and proportions, and dividing mass by flipper length does not necessarily remove those differences.
This workflow demonstrates two-way data exchange:

R → Python: penguins_data and overall_corr.
Python → R: penguins_bci and bci_profile.

R handles loading, ranking, and visualization, while Python performs species-level correlations and BCI calculations.
